lead: A shallow network has one or two hidden layers. A deep network has many, and each layer builds its features from the layer below: edges become parts, parts become objects. The catch is that backpropagation through many sigmoid layers multiplies the gradient by a small fraction at every layer, so the early layers barely learn. ReLU units, careful initialization and shortcut connections keep that gradient alive. Most modern image, speech and medical-imaging models build on these ideas in some form, usually combined with normalization and skip connections.
prereq: You need: hidden layers and activation functions from chapters 5.3 and 5.4, and the chain rule of backpropagation from 5.5.

blocks.text: Take an image of a chest X-ray. The first hidden layer responds to short dark or bright edges. The second combines those edges into corners and blobs. The third combines blobs into shapes such as a rib line or a heart border. Later layers combine shapes into a diagnosis. Nobody wrote those features by hand; backpropagation found them. That is the main claim of deep learning: features composed from features, learned from data.

Older computer vision built features by hand, such as edge filters and texture histograms, and fed the numbers to a separate classifier. A deep network replaces that pipeline with many layers of simple units and trains the whole thing end to end.

The wording matters in exams. An artificial neural network (ANN) is any network of artificial neurons, and a single perceptron counts. Deep learning is the practice of training networks with many hidden layers, where the representations are learned, using large datasets and GPU hardware. Depth is the number of layers on the longest path from input to output, not the number of weights: a very wide one-hidden-layer network is still shallow. Deep networks can represent some functions with far fewer units than a shallow network needs; that is a representational advantage. The practical arrival of deep networks came from large datasets, GPU hardware and better training tricks.

Backpropagation multiplies local derivatives along the path from the loss back to a weight. For a sigmoid unit σ(z) = 1/(1+e^(−z)) the local derivative is σ′(z) = σ(z)(1 − σ(z)). It is largest at z = 0, where σ = 0.5 and σ′ = 0.25. So the best a sigmoid layer can do is pass one quarter of the gradient. Every extra layer multiplies the signal by at most 0.25.

blocks.where: L is the loss, W₁ the weights of the first layer, a_L the last activation, z_l the pre-activation of layer l, W_l its weight matrix, σ′ the sigmoid derivative, and Π_{l=2..L} the product taken from the last layer back to layer 2. Every layer in the product contributes both its sigmoid derivative and its weight matrix.

blocks.text: Five layers give 0.25⁵ ≈ 0.001. Ten layers give about 9.5×10⁻⁷. The gradient reaching the first layer is practically zero, so those weights stop moving. Older texts call this unit saturation: when |z| is large the sigmoid is flat, σ′ → 0, and the unit is saturated, meaning it neither learns nor passes gradient.

The reverse case is exploding gradients. If the weight matrices are large, the same product of terms above 1 grows without bound and the weights jump around instead of settling. One product of many numbers causes both effects. Saturated sigmoid units are the usual cause, and the vanishing gradient is the effect seen across many layers.

ReLU(z) = max(0, z). Its derivative is 1 for z > 0 and 0 for z < 0. On the active side the layer passes the gradient unchanged, so a chain of active ReLU units has factor 1^L = 1 and the first layer learns as fast as the last. It is also cheap: one comparison, no exponential.

items: Leaky ReLU uses 0.01z for z < 0, so a negative unit still carries a small gradient; ELU and its relatives smooth that corner.

ReLU has its own failure. A unit whose pre-activation is negative for every input passes zero gradient, so its weights never change again. That is a dead unit. Leaky ReLU and a sensible learning rate reduce it.

Xavier (Glorot) initialization sets the weight variance to 2/(fan_in + fan_out) for sigmoid and tanh layers. He initialization sets it to 2/fan_in for ReLU layers, because about half the units are silent. fan_in is the number of inputs to a unit.

blocks.text: Residual connection: instead of a block computing y = F(x), it computes y = F(x) + x. The gradient now has a path with derivative 1 straight back to the input, so it no longer has to survive every layer as a product. Only a few curricula teach this at this level; most exams ask for the one-line statement.

figure.caption: Each layer back multiplies the gradient by the best-case sigmoid derivative 0.25, so that curve collapses towards zero by layer five; the flat line is a chain of active ReLU units, which pass the gradient unchanged.

spec.aria: The sigmoid chain curve falls steeply towards zero over ten layers while the ReLU chain stays flat at one.

examples.question: A network has five sigmoid layers between a weight w in the first layer and the loss. The gradient of the loss with respect to the output activation is 1.0. (a) Give the best-case shrink factor over the five layers. (b) Give the gradient that reaches w. (c) With learning rate η = 0.1, how far does w move in one step? (d) Repeat (b) and (c) for five ReLU layers whose pre-activations are all positive.
steps: Best case for one sigmoid layer: z = 0, so σ′ = σ(1−σ) = 0.5 × 0.5 = 0.25.
(c) Weight step: Δw = η × gradient = 0.1 × 0.0009765625 = 9.765625×10⁻⁵, about 0.0001 per step.
(d) ReLU: derivative is 1 for z > 0, so the factor is 1⁵ = 1. The gradient arrives as 1.0 × 1 = 1.0.
Weight step with ReLU: Δw = 0.1 × 1.0 = 0.1, which is 1024 times larger than the sigmoid step.
examples.answer: The sigmoid stack delivers 0.00098 of a gradient of 1.0 and moves the weight by 9.77×10⁻⁵ per step, while the ReLU stack delivers 1.0 and moves it by 0.1.
examples.check:
eta = 0.1
factor = 0.25 ** 5
g_sig = 1.0 * factor
g_relu = 1.0 * (1.0 ** 5)
step_sig = eta * g_sig
step_relu = eta * g_relu
print(factor)
print(g_sig)
print(step_sig)
print(g_relu)
print(step_relu)

traps: Deep learning is not more epochs or a bigger batch. Trained for 500 epochs, a one-hidden-layer network is still shallow. Depth means layers of learned features.
The maximum slope of a sigmoid is 0.25, but the maximum slope of tanh is 1.0. Mixing the two turns the correct factor 0.25^L into a wrong 1/L.
ReLU does not remove vanishing gradients everywhere. A unit with z < 0 for all inputs has derivative 0, receives nothing and stays dead on its own.
Vanishing and exploding gradients are the same product: factors below 1 shrink it, factors above 1 blow it up. Neither is caused by the loss function alone.
Depth is counted in layers, not parameters. A wide shallow network can hold more weights than a small deep one and still be called shallow.

quiz.q: State the ReLU function and its derivative for z > 0 and for z < 0.
quiz.a: ReLU(z) = max(0, z). The derivative is 1 for z > 0 and 0 for z < 0; at z = 0 it is not defined and is taken as 0.

quiz.q: What is the largest value of σ′(z) for the logistic sigmoid, and at which z does it occur?
Why does the gradient fall off exponentially with depth in a stack of sigmoid layers?
quiz.a: Each layer multiplies the backward signal by σ′(z), which is at most 0.25. Over L layers the factor is at most 0.25^L, which shrinks fast with L, so the gradient reaching the early layers is tiny.

quiz.q: A gradient of 1.0 must travel back through eight sigmoid layers at the best-case derivative. What reaches the first layer? What would reach it through eight ReLU layers with positive pre-activations?
quiz.a: Sigmoid factor: 0.25⁸ = 1.52587890625×10⁻⁵, so about 1.53×10⁻⁵ arrives. ReLU factor: 1⁸ = 1, so the full 1.0 arrives, roughly 65536 times larger.

quiz.q: A ReLU unit has pre-activation z = −2.5. Give its output and the gradient that passes through it. What happens to the unit during training?
quiz.a: Output max(0, −2.5) = 0. Derivative 0, so no gradient passes. The unit receives no update and stays inactive while its pre-activation remains negative.

quiz.q: Explain why a residual connection y = F(x) + x helps the gradient reach the early layers.
quiz.a: Differentiating gives ∂y/∂x = ∂F/∂x + I, an identity path with derivative 1. The gradient reaching the input is a sum of terms, one of which needs no product of layer derivatives, so it does not shrink by 0.25 per layer.

quiz.q: Why does He initialization use variance 2/fan_in while Xavier uses 2/(fan_in + fan_out)?
quiz.a: ReLU sets about half the units to zero, which halves the variance of the outputs. Doubling the starting variance with 2/fan_in restores it, so activations keep roughly constant scale across layers. Xavier assumes symmetric activations such as sigmoid or tanh and balances the signal in both the forward and backward directions.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern architectures rarely stack plain sigmoids; they use normalization layers, residual blocks and the ReLU family almost everywhere. Transformer models for text and vision also carry skip connections and normalization at every block. Depth-separation theory studies how many more units a shallow network needs for the same function. Useful search terms: dying ReLU, He initialization, ResNet skip connection, batch normalization. Medical case studies, such as heart disease risk prediction from tabular records, apply the same shallow-to-deep trade-off on much smaller data.
